To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the F11 antigen is a glycoprotein that can be biosynthesized by melanoma and neuroblastoma cells and that the F11 antibody recognizes an epitope on the 100K antigen that is present on the cell surface of melanoma cells but is absent from the surface of normal melanocytes.

the molecular profiles of glycoprotein antigengen recognized by the monoclonal antibody, F11, are different in melanoma and neuroblastoma cell lines and that the antigenic site recognized on these glycoproteins is common to both melanoma and neuro-blastoma.
the molecular profiles of glycoprotein antigencs recognized by the monoclonal antibody, F11, are different when isolated from the cell associated or secreted antigens of melanoma cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the molecular profiles of melanocyte and melanoma antigens recognized by a panel of monoclonal antibodies (MAb).
the characterization and definition of melanoma-associated antigens recognized by the monoclonal antibody, F11, originally made to a spent medium antigen of human melanoma cells.
the characterization of a melanoma-associated antigen recognized by the monoclonal antibody, F11.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
monoclonal antibody 11 defines a glycoprotein antigen on melanoma cells that is biosynthetically related to other melanoma antigens but structurally distinct from the antigen on a neuroblastoma.

the F11 antigen, which is recognized by a monoclonal antibody, is a sialoglycopeptide of 100,000 molecular weight which is synthesized by melanoma and neuroblastoma cells and secreted into the culture media.

the antigenic determinants recognized by monoclonals are not necessarily identical in structure or function, and that the antigenic sites recognized by monoclonally produced antibodies are not necessarily identical with the antigenic determinates recognized by polyclonally produced antibodies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a monoclonal antibody (F11) made to a partially-purified spent media antigen of human melanoma cells was used to define the molecular profiles of cell-associated and spent media glycoprotein antigents of melanoma and neuroblastoma cells.
the F11 antigen appears to be a glycosylated form of the 75 K glycoprotein.
the antigenic sites on the 75 and/or 77 K glycoproteins are not exposed on the surface of the melanoma cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a monoclonal antibody can define an antigenic site on a glycoprotein that is expressed on a variety of different cell types.
a single monoclonal antibody, F11, can recognize a number of structurally distinct antigens on different melanoma cells.
a monoclonal antibody originally made against a spent medium antigen of human melanoma cells, F11, recognizes a cell associated antigen of Mr 75-77 K in detergent lysates of the same melanoma cells.
